content: Teenage motherhood and failure to complete high school significantly limit career opportunities for many young women. Research from 1988 revealed that 60% of teenage mothers were living in poverty at the time of giving birth. Further studies indicate that nearly half of all adolescent mothers seek social assistance within the first five years of their child’s life. A study conducted in the United Kingdom involving 100 teenage mothers found that only 11% were employed, while the remaining 89% were unemployed. Most British teenage mothers live in poverty, with nearly half falling into the lowest fifth of the income distribution. Additionally, one-quarter of adolescent mothers have a second child within 24 months of their first. Factors influencing the likelihood of closely spaced repeat births include marital status and education level. The probability of a repeat birth decreases with higher levels of education, either of the young woman or her parents, but increases if the young woman is married. Early motherhood can have profound effects on the psychosocial development of the infant. Children born to teenage mothers are at an increased risk of developmental disabilities and behavioral issues. Studies suggest that adolescent mothers are less likely to engage in affectionate behaviors such as touch, smiling, and verbal communication with their infants, and they may be less sensitive and accepting of their child’s needs. However, those with greater social support are less likely to exhibit anger toward their children or rely on punitive measures. Academic underperformance is also more common among children of teenage mothers, with many failing to graduate from secondary school, being held back a grade, or scoring lower on standardized tests. Daughters of adolescent parents are more likely to become teenage mothers themselves, while sons born to teenage mothers are three times more likely to serve time in prison. Teen pregnancy and motherhood can also impact younger siblings. Research shows that younger sisters of teenage mothers are less likely to prioritize education and employment and are more likely to accept early sexual initiation, parenthood, and marriage. Younger brothers, similarly, are more tolerant of non-marital and early births and are more prone to engage in high-risk behaviors. Another study found that younger siblings of teenage parents often take on babysitting responsibilities for their nieces and nephews, which increases the risk of early pregnancy for young girls in such situations. In some cases, the father of the child is the teenage girl’s husband, with conception occurring within marriage or the pregnancy leading to marriage (commonly referred to as a shotgun wedding). In countries like India and Greece, most teenage births occur within marriage, whereas in countries like the United States and Ireland, the majority of teenage mothers are not married to the fathers of their children. In the UK, half of all teenage parents are single parents, 40% cohabit as a couple, and 10% are married. While many teenage parents are in romantic relationships at the time of birth, adolescent fathers often do not remain with the mother, which can disrupt their relationship with the child. Studies show that teenage fathers who are involved in decision-making during pregnancy and birth are more likely to remain engaged with their children in later years. However, eight out of ten teenage fathers in the United States do not marry the mother of their child. Notably, the term teenage father may be misleading, as studies reveal that two-thirds of births to teenage girls in the U.S. are fathered by adult men aged 20 or older. Similarly, in the UK, 72% of jointly registered births to women under 20 involve fathers over 20, with nearly one in four being over 25. Teenage pregnancy has also been a recurring theme in literature, film, and television. These portrayals range from historical settings (e.g., The Blue Lagoon) to contemporary ones (e.g., One Tree Hill). While the subject is often treated seriously (e.g., Junk), it can also be depicted in a comedic manner, playing on stereotypes (e.g., Vicky Pollard in Little Britain). The circumstances of the pregnancy vary, from sexual abuse (e.g., Rose in The Cider House Rules) to one-night stands (e.g., Amy Barnes in Hollyoaks) or romantic relationships (e.g., Demi Miller in EastEnders). Some narratives explore the decision-making process surrounding abortion (e.g., Fast Times at Ridgemont High), adoption (e.g., Mom at Sixteen, Juno), marriage (e.g., Reba and Jeni, Juno), or single motherhood (e.g., Someone Like You). In Spring Awakening, the central female character dies from a botched abortion, while Stephanie Daley examines the aftermath of a teenage pregnancy ending in the death of a newborn. Other works, such as Too Young to Be a Dad, focus on the teenage father, while The Snapper highlights the family’s reactions, particularly the soon-to-be grandfather. The 2007 Oscar-nominated film Juno follows a young teenage girl navigating her pregnancy. Long-running television series like Degrassi Junior High explore the long-term effects of teenage parenthood, while Gilmore Girls portrays the unique dynamic between a teenage mother and her daughter, who are only 16 years apart. Looking for Alibrandi features the teenage daughter of a woman who was herself a teenage mother. Songs addressing teenage pregnancy range from somber tales of abuse (e.g., Brenda’s Got a Baby), poverty (e.g., In the Ghetto), and back-alley abortions (e.g., Sally’s Pigeons) to defiant and upbeat tracks like Papa Don’t Preach. American pop singer Fantasia Barrino, who became a mother at 17, released a controversial song titled Baby Mama, which highlights the challenges of single motherhood, including financial and familial struggles.
